sentences.text: 2. Brief facts of the case are that on 26.02.2018, father of the prosecutrix has lodged a missing report to the Police Station Chhura, District-Gariyaband to the effect that his daughter (hereafter, referred to as 'the prosecutrix'), who is aged about 15 years 8 months, went somewhere after leaving a letter dated 25.02.2018 at about 11 A.M and has not returned back to his house.
The Police registered offence punishable under Section 363 of the CrPC against unknown persons.
During the course of investigation, prosecutrix was recovered on 26.08.2019 from the possession of the appellant and recovery Panchnama (ExP4) was prepared.

Prosecutrix was sent for medical examination to the District Hospital, Gariyaband, where Dr Abha Chaturvedi (PW12) examined her and gave MLC report (ExP21), wherein she opined that at the time of examination, prosecutrix was on her periods,
and therefore, she could not be examined.

With regard to the age of the prosecutrix, Police seized the progress report of Class 8 th (Article-1) of the prosecutrix from the Saraswati Shishu Mandir,
Chhura, District-Surguja (SSM Chhura) vide ExP3, a Certificate was also seized which was issued by the head Master of the School, with respect to the date of birth of the prosecutrix.
The School Admission and Discharge Register from the SSM Chhura has also been seized by the Police and copy of the School Admission and Discharge Register is referred to as Article-2(c).
The letter that was left by the prosecutrix in her house while Cra 793 of 2022 she was leaving the house was also seized and marked as Article-3.
Statement of the prosecutrix and other witnesses have been recorded under Section 161 of the CrPC.
Appellant was arrested and he was also sent for his medical examination to the District Hospital, Gariyaband, and after examination, report (ExP14) was obtained by the Police.

After completion of investigation, charge-sheet was filed before the Additional Sessions Judge,
Gariyaband on 19.11.2019 against the appellant for the offence punishable under Sections 363, 366,
376(2)(n), 376(3), 294, 323, 506 Part-II, 342 and 365 of the IPC and Section 6 of the POCSO Act.

Trial Court has framed charges under Sections 363, 366, 376(2)(n), 376(3), 294, 323, 506 Part-II,
342 and 365 of the IPC and Section 6 of the POCSO Act.
The accused abjured his guilt and pleaded innocence.
3. In order to establish the charges framed against the appellant, prosecution has examined as many as 13 witnesses.

Statement of the appellant under Section 313 of the CrPC was also recorded in which he denied the material appearing against him, and pleaded that he is innocent and has been falsely implicated in the case.
After appreciation of the evidence available on record the learned trial Court convicted the appellant and sentenced him as mentioned in para-1 of this judgment.
Hence this appeal.
4. Learned counsel for the appellant would submit that prosecution has failed to prove the case against the appellant beyond reasonable doubt.
There is no legal and admissible evidence on record with regard to the age of the prosecutrix that on the date of incident, she was minor and less than 18 years of age.
In absence of examination of author of Cra 793 of 2022 the School Admission and Discharge Register, the same cannot be taken into consideration for determination of the age of the prosecutrix.
School Admission and Discharge Register is very weak type of evidence.
There appears no any Kotwari Register or ossification report to determine the actual age of the prosecutrix i.e. that on the date of incident, she was below 18 years of age.

While her staying in Kodobhata, Raigarh with the appellant, she has not made any complaint to any person of nearby place, therefore, the alleged offence committed under Sections of IPC and POCSO Act against the appellant are not made out and he is entitled for acquittal.

6. On the other hand, learned State counsel opposed the argument of learned counsel for the appellant and submitted that prosecutrix was minor, and below 18 years at the time of incident,
which is proved by the School Admission and Discharge Register, which contains the date of birth of prosecutrix as 24.06.2002.

The School Register is admissible piece of evidence to determine age of the prosecutrix, therefore, there is no illegality or infirmity in the finding of the learned trial court that the prosecutrix was abducted by the appellant and kept with him, away from Cra 793 of 2022 the lawful guardianship for a considerable period, and committed forceful sexual intercourse with her therefore, impugned judgment needs no interference.
7. We have heard learned counsel for the parties and perused the material available on record, with utmost circumference.
8. In order to consider the age of the prosecutrix, we have examined the evidence available on record produced by the prosecution.
The prosecution has relied upon the School Admission and Discharge Register, Article 2(c), which is proved by PW7 Khuleshwar Prasad Sahu, who was the In-charge Head Master of the SSM Chhura.

He stated in his deposition that he came along with the original Admission and Discharge Register in which date of birth of the prosecutrix is mentioned as 24.06.2002, and copy of the same is Article 2(c).

In his cross examination, he stated that at the time of admission of the prosectrix in the school, no document relating to her date of birth was produced and he could tell the date of birth of the prosecutrix only on the basis of available record i.e. the School Admission and Discharge Register.
PW5 Suresh Kumar Yadav was working as Principal of SSM Chhura from the year 2012 to 2018.
He stated that he has issued certificate with respect to date of birth of the prosecutrix which is Ex.P7.
He admits in his cross examination that on the basis of the School Admission and Discharge Register, he issued the Certificate Ex.P7 and he is the friend of the father of the prosecutrix.
PW1 is father of the prosecutrix, who stated in his evidence that date of birth of his daughter is 24.06.2002.

In his cross examination, he admits that after birth of the child,
the information Cra 793 of 2022 regarding birth of the child is to be recorded at Anganbadi Centre,
but it is also admitted by him that he has not recorded the birth of his child i.e. prosecutrix at Panchayat, Anganwadi Centre, or Kotwari Register and had not obtained any Birth Certificate.
He further stated that he could not remember as to on which year he had admitted the prosecutrix in the School.
PW2 is mother of the prosecutrix.
She too stated in her evidence that date of birth of the prosecutrix is 24.06.2002.

In her cross examination, she also admitted that there is no endorsement with respect to date of birth of her child, i.e. prosecutrix, at Panchayat, or in Kotwari Register, and she further admitted that she has not obtained any Birth Certificate of the prosecurix from anywhere.

sentences.text: 9. After considering the entire evidence and facts and circumstances of the case, it emerges that the prosecution has failed to produce any cogent and reliable evidence with respect to the date of birth of the prosecutrix.
The prosecution is silent as to the process, by which the date of birth of the prosecutrix was recorded in the school Admission and Discharge Register.

There are material contradictions on the evidence of mother and father of the prosecutrix as well as, the Headmasters of the school who have issued the certificate and the copy of the School Admission and Discharge Register.
In the matter of Ravinder Singh Gorkhi Vs State of UP and Others reported in 2006 (5) SCC 584 Hon'ble Supreme Court has observed the following in Para 26:

In Birad Mal Singhvi v. Anand Purohit [(1988 Supp. SCC 604], this Court held:
"To render a document admissible under Section 35, three conditions must be satisfied, firstly, entry that is relied on must be one in a public or other official book,
register or record; secondly, it must be an entry stating a fact in issue or relevant fact;
and thirdly, it must be made by a public servant in discharge of his official duty, or any other person in performance of a duty specially enjoined by law.

sentences.text: The age of a person as recorded in the school register or otherwise may be used for various purposes, namely, for obtaining admission; for obtaining an appointment; for contesting election; registration of marriage; obtaining a separate unit under the ceiling laws; and even for the purpose of litigating before a civil forum e.g. necessity of being represented in a court of law by a guardian or where a suit is filed on the ground that the plaintiff being a minor he was not appropriately represented therein or any transaction made on his behalf was void as he was a minor.
A court of law for the purpose of determining the age of a (2006) 5 SCC 584 party to the lis, having regard to the provisions of Section 35 of the Evidence Act will have to apply the same standard.

No different standard can be applied in case of an accused as in a case of abduction or rape, or similar offence where the victim or the prosecutrix although might have consented with the accused, if on the basis of the entries made in the register maintained by the school, a judgment of conviction is recorded, the accused would be deprived of his constitutional right under Article 21 of the Constitution, as in that case the accused may unjustly be convicted."

sentences.text: The said presumption is however not conclusive proof of the age of juvenility and the same may be rebutted by contra evidence let in by the opposite side.

33.5. That the procedure of an inquiry by a Court is not the same thing as declaring the age of the person as a juvenile sought before the JJ Board when the case is pending for trial before the concerned criminal court.

In case of an inquiry, the Court records a prima facie conclusion but when there is a determination of age as per sub-section (2) of section 94 of 2015 Act, a declaration is made on the basis of evidence.
Also the age recorded by the JJ Board shall be deemed to be the true age of the person brought before it.

Thus, the standard of proof in an inquiry is different from that required in a proceeding where the determination and declaration of the age of a person has to be made on the basis of evidence scrutinised and accepted only if worthy of such acceptance.
33.6. That it is neither feasible nor desirable to lay down an abstract formula to determine the age of a person.
It has to be on the basis of the material on record and on appreciation of evidence adduced by the parties in each case.
33.7 This Court has observed that a hypertechnical approach should not be adopted when evidence is adduced on behalf of the accused in support of the plea that he was a juvenile.
33.8. If two views are possible on the same evidence, the court should lean in favour of holding the accused to be a juvenile in borderline cases.

This is in order to ensure that the benefit of the JJ Act,
2015 is made applicable to the juvenile in conflict with law.
At the same time, the Court Cra 793 of 2022 should ensure that the JJ Act, 2015 is not misused by persons to escape punishment after having committed serious offences.

33.9. That when the determination of age is on the basis of evidence such as school records, it is necessary that the same would have to be considered as per Section 35 of the Indian Evidence Act, inasmuch as any public or official document maintained in the discharge of official duty would have greater credibility than private documents.

Any document which is in consonance with public documents, such as matriculation certificate, could be accepted by the Court or the JJ Board provided such public document is credible and authentic as per the provisions of the Indian Evidence Act viz., section 35 and other provisions.

33.11. Ossification Test cannot be the sole criterion for age determination and a mechanical view regarding the age of a person cannot be adopted solely on the basis of medical opinion by radiological examination.
Such evidence is not conclusive evidence but only a very useful guiding factor to be considered in the absence of documents mentioned in Section 94(2) of the JJ Act, 2015."

15. In a recent decision, in Rishipal Singh Solanki vs. State of Uttar Pradesh & Ors. this court outlined the procedure to be followed in cases where age determination is required.

The court was dealing with Rule 12 of the erstwhile Juvenile Justice Rules (which is in pari materia) with Section 94 of the JJ Act, and held as follows:
"20. Rule 12 of the JJ Rules, 2007 deals with the procedure to be followed in determination of age.
The juvenility of a person in conflict with law had to be decided prima facie on the basis of physical appearance, or documents, if available.

But an inquiry into the determination of age by the Court or the JJ Board was by seeking evidence by obtaining: (i) the matriculation or equivalent certificates, if available and in the absence whereof; (ii) the date of birth certificate from the school (other than a play school) first attended; and in the absence whereof; (iii) the birth certificate given by a corporation or a municipal authority or a panchayat.
Only in the absence of either (i), (ii) and (iii) above, the medical opinion could be sought from a duly constituted Medical Board to declare the age of the juvenile or child.

It was also provided that while determination was being made, benefit could be given to the child or juvenile by considering the age on lower side within the margin of one year."

15. Reverting to the facts of the present case, on due consideration of the prosecution evidence, we find that no clinching and legally admissible evidence has been brought by the prosecution to prove the fact that prosecutrix was minor on the date of incident.
Despite that the trial court in the impugned judgment, has held her minor.

Hence, we set aside the finding given by the trial Court that on the date of incident, the victim was minor, as the same has not been proved by the prosecution by leading clinching and cogent evidence.
16. So far as the issue of forceable intercourse of the appellant with the prosecutrix is concerned, we have carefully perused the statement of the prosecutrix, PW3.
She stated in her deposition that on 25.02.2018, that she was called by the appellant from her school and after enticing her, he has taken her to Raighar, Odisha.
The appellant has taken her from Chhura to Odisha on his motor cycle.
She resided along with the appellant at Village Kodobhata, Raighar in a rented house where he was making physical relationship with her.
They stayed there for about one Cra 793 of 2022 and half years.
She delivered a girl child from the appellant who was aged about 10 months at the time of her recovery from Odisha.
In the month of August 2019, the Police went there to Odisha, and taken the prosecutrix along with the appellant.
In her cross examination, she stated that she was regularly in contact with the appellant through mobile phone while she was studying at school.
She admits that upon asking by the appellant to sit on his motorcycle, she did so and went with him on his motorcycle.
She further admits that the appellant had not used any force while she was sitting on his vehicle and she herself was sitting behind him on his motorcycle.
She admits that on their way to Kodobhata, there are so many villages.

Appellant and the prosecutrix have crossed those villages,
where many people are also there.
She also admits that on the way to Gariyaband also, they crossed many cities.
She further admits that she has not tried to get herself out from the clutches of the appellant and had not tried to get any help of any other person at Gariyaband.
Despite having sufficient opportunity while staying with the appellant at Odisha, the prosecutrix has not made any complaint to any person of her nearby place or adjoining house.
Dr Abha Chaturvedi, who has examined the prosecutrix has not found any injury on her private parts, either external or internal, and further, there was no sign of any forceable sexual intercourse.

sentences.text: 18. PW9, who is the Investigation Officer has stated in his evidence that on 19.03.2018, he seized the letter written by the prosecutrix Article-3 from father of the prosecutrix.
It reveals from the letter that prosecutrix was in love affair with the appellant.

The prosecutrix was having grudge Cra 793 of 2022 against her family members and she herself left her house on her own will, after leaving the letter, Article-3.
19.

Close scrutiny of the evidence makes it clear that prosecutrix is a consenting party, and she herself went along with the appellant from Chhura to Odisha on his motor cycle and stayed there for a considerable period i.e. 1  years.
She did not ask for any help from anybody of nearby place or she informed to any of the persons while going from Chhura to Odisha.
Neither she was taken by force nor abducted by the appellant.
She herself accompanied the appellant on her own will, wish and with consent.
Further it is also not a case that the appellant committed forceable physical relationship with the prosecutrix without her will and consent.

20. With respect to the offence punishable under Section 294 IPC, for which the appellant is also convicted and sentenced, after perusal of the deposition of the prosecutrix (PW1), it appears that in her deposition there is absolutely no evidence with respect to any obscene act or song by the accused person by which, prosecutrix was annoyed.
Even no using of any filthy language has been deposed by the prosecutrix in her deposition.
Therefore, conviction of the appellant under Section 294 of the IPC is erroneous.

Likewise, with respect to conviction under Section 506 Part-II of the IPC, in para-12 of deposition of the prosecutrix, she has only said that whenever she made request to the appellant for returning to her parents' house, appellant threatened her.

This court is of the opinion that one line sentence would not be sufficient to held the appellant guilty for the offence punishable under Section 506 Part-II of Cra 793 of 2022 the IPC and something more is required to substantiate the allegation for criminal intimidation or threat to cause death or grievous hurt,
therefore, offence punishable under Section 506 Part-II is also not made out against the appellant.

21. So far as the allegation of assault made by the appellant on prosecutrix is concerned, prosecutrix has stated in her deposition that appellant assaulted her usually and has not permitted her to go outside from the house.
In her cross-examination, she reiterated her conversion that appellant used to beat her normally.
She further stated that appellant locked the door of the house from outside.

Nothing has been elicited by the defence in the deposition of prosecutrix so as to make the statement of prosecutrix doubtful with respect to the offence punishable under Sections 323 and 342 of the IPC.

PW12 Dr Abha Chaturvedi, while examining the prosecutrix, has noticed old mark of injury on the back of her right hand, which was already healed, which corroborates statement of the prosecutrix that appellant used to assault her.

22. Considering the entire evidence available on record, particularly, the evidence with regard to the age of the prosecutrix, and her conduct, we are of the opinion that the prosecutrix was more than 18 years of age at the time of incident, and further, she was a consenting party with the appellant,
therefore, in the above facts and circumstances, the offence punishable under Sections 363, 366,
376(2)(n), 376(3), 294, and 506 Part-II, of the IPC and Section 6 of the POCSO Act would not be made out against the appellant.

4 Evidence Act.
However, the admissibility of such a document would be of not much evidentiary value to prove the age of the girl in the absence of the material on the basis of which the age was recorded.
However, the documents mentioned in Rule 12(3)(a)(i), (ii), and (iii) of the JJ Rules 2007 made under the JJ Act, 2000 or sub-section (2) of section 94 of JJ Act, 2015, shall be sufficient for prima facie satisfaction of the Court.

5 33.4.
33.5. That the procedure of an inquiry by a Court is not the same thing as declaring the age of the person as a juvenile sought before the JJ Board when the case is pending for trial before the concerned criminal court.
In case of an inquiry, the Court records a prima facie conclusion but when there is a determination of age as per sub-section (2) of section 94 of 2015 Act, a declaration is made on the basis of evidence.
Also the age recorded by the JJ Board shall be deemed to be the true age of the person brought before it.
Thus, the standard of proof in an inquiry is different from that required in a proceeding where the determination and declaration of the age of a person has to be made on the basis of evidence scrutinised and accepted only if worthy of such acceptance.
It has to be on the basis of the material on record and on appreciation of evidence adduced by the parties in each case.
Section 94 (2)(iii) of the JJ Act clearly indicates that the date of birth certificate from the school or matriculation or equivalent certificate by the concerned examination board has to be firstly preferred in the absence of which the birth certificate issued by the Corporation or Municipal Authority or Panchayat and it is only thereafter in the absence of these such documents the age is to be determined Bhakt Prahalad @ Ankit Sonwani vs State Of Chhattisgarh on 15 December, 2023 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/173932326/
6 through "an ossification test" or "any other latest medical age determination test"
conducted on the orders of the concerned authority, i.e. Committee or Board or Court.
The burden is always upon the prosecution to establish what it alleges; therefore, the prosecution could not have been fallen back upon a document which it had never relied upon.

Hence, we set aside the finding given by the trial Court that on the date of incident, the victim was minor, as the same has not been proved by the prosecution by leading clinching and cogent evidence.
Neither she was taken by force nor abducted by the appellant.
Further it is also not a case that the appellant committed forceable physical relationship with the prosecutrix without her will and consent.
Therefore, conviction of the appellant under Section 294 of the IPC is erroneous.
This court is of the opinion that one line sentence would not be sufficient to held the appellant guilty for the offence punishable under Section 506 Part-II of Cra 793 of 2022 the IPC and something more is required to substantiate the allegation for criminal intimidation or threat to cause death or grievous hurt,
therefore, offence punishable under Section 506 Part-II is also not made out against the appellant.
However, the offence punishable under Sections 323 and 342 IPC is made out against the appellant.
